title: Evolution, Not Revolution: Why China Isn’t Pushing Its Cleantech Advantage in the Hormuz Crisis | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Oil prices rose far less than analysts expected after the Strait of Hormuz closure primarily because China slashed its fossil fuel imports, and CFR's David Hart argues the reason is arithmetic rather than climate strategy: China's $220 billion of 2025 cleantech exports are only 6 percent of its $3.77 trillion export total, so high oil prices destroy far more demand for Chinese electronics, textiles, metals and chemicals than they create for solar, batteries and EVs. He expects the crisis to accelerate cleantech adoption over time as import-dependent countries de-risk from petroleum — an evolution, not a revolution.

insights.claim: The most surprising outcome of the Strait of Hormuz crisis is that oil prices have not risen nearly as much as many analysts expected, and the biggest single reason is that China cut its fossil fuel imports massively in the months since the closure.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Chinese import behavior, not OPEC spare capacity, is the marginal variable suppressing crude prices during this crisis — track Chinese crude and LNG import volumes as the key price signal.
insights.quote: The biggest reason is that China cut its fossil fuel imports massively
insights.locator: Yet, the most surprising outcome of the Strait of Hormuz crisis

insights.claim: Some quarters of the climate movement felt perverse optimism when the Hormuz closure raised oil prices, since Donald Trump had inadvertently accomplished the movement's dream of expensive oil.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Frames the consensus expectation the article overturns: high oil was assumed to be an automatic tailwind for the energy transition.
insights.quote: The movement’s archenemy, U.S. President Donald Trump, had, in one fell swoop, accomplished its dream of raising the price of oil.

themes.theme: China's export arithmetic beats cleantech leverage

insights.claim: China exported about $220 billion of solar panels, electric vehicles, batteries and wind turbines in 2025 — only 6 percent of its $3.77 trillion total exports, meaning cleantech is far too small a share to justify maximizing fossil-consumer pain.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: The hard ratio that caps how far China will weaponize its cleantech position — cleantech is a rounding error against its broader export book.
insights.quote: In 2025, China exported about $220 billion worth of solar panels, electric vehicles, batteries, and wind turbines. That sounds like a lot, and it is. But it’s only 6 percent of the $3.77 trillion that China exported overall.
insights.locator: All these speculations need to be seen in the light

insights.claim: China is the leading trade partner of more than 120 countries, and every additional dollar those countries spend on imported oil and LNG because of the Hormuz crisis is a dollar not spent on Chinese electronics, textiles, metals and chemicals — categories worth hundreds of billions more than the 'new three' cleantech exports.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: High oil is a direct demand tax on Chinese general-goods exports — the transmission channel that makes Beijing an oil-price dove regardless of its cleantech position.
insights.quote: Every additional dollar that those countries spend on imported oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) because of the Strait of Hormuz crisis isn’t being spent on Chinese electronics, textiles, metals, and chemicals
insights.locator: China is the leading trade partner of more than 120 countries

insights.claim: Political explanations for China's restraint — valuing stability, wanting to be seen as the adult in the room, seeking a reciprocal favor from the Trump administration, or preferring continued Republican control — are secondary to the cold economic fact that China exports far more than cleantech.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Use trade-composition math rather than geopolitical intent-reading to forecast Chinese behavior in energy crises.
insights.quote: All these speculations need to be seen in the light of a cold, hard economic fact: China exports more than cleantech. A lot more.
insights.locator: Many political analysts have proposed answers

insights.claim: China is in desperate need of export revenues because its economy has slowed considerably, it appears unable to boost domestic demand, and exports account for virtually all of its economic growth — while it also saves money on its remaining oil and LNG imports.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: China's growth model leaves it structurally dependent on foreign purchasing power, so it will act to suppress oil prices — a persistent dampener on crude upside.
insights.quote: Exports account for virtually all its economic growth.
insights.locator: China is in desperate need of export revenues

themes.theme: Global growth drag from high oil

insights.claim: Rising oil prices are slowing global economic growth and could trigger an economic crisis if they go too high, with knock-on effects for Chinese exports.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Links the oil price directly to Chinese export demand — a feedback loop that gives Beijing a self-interested cap on how high it lets crude run.
insights.locator: Moreover, the rising price of oil is slowing global economic growth

insights.claim: The IMF's most recent outlook, which assumed the Strait of Hormuz would reopen in mid-July, forecast global growth of only 3 percent in 2026, shrinking to 2 percent if the strait remained closed amid sustained hostilities, with the steepest slowdown in emerging markets.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: A concrete 100bp global growth haircut tied to Hormuz closure duration, with emerging markets as the concentrated pain point — a direct EM risk input.
insights.quote: forecasted global growth of only 3 percent in 2026, shrinking to 2 percent if the strait remained closed amid sustained hostilities
insights.locator: The International Monetary Fund’s most recent economic outlook

insights.claim: In the long run the Hormuz crisis is likely to accelerate cleantech adoption, much of it imported from China, because renewables plus batteries plus electric cars relieve petroleum-importing countries of an economic risk the crisis has proven all too real.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Energy-security motive, not climate policy, becomes the durable demand driver for Chinese cleantech exports into import-dependent economies.
insights.locator: In the long run, the crisis is likely to accelerate

insights.claim: The renewables-batteries-EV package keeps getting more affordable even as performance improves, and importing countries may dislike growing dependence on China but a cleantech supply cutoff would be far less severe immediately than having their current energy systems starved of fuel.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Explains why China-dependency concerns will not stop cleantech imports: the failure mode of a cleantech embargo is far milder than a fuel embargo.
insights.quote: even if cleantech imports were cut off, the immediate consequences would be far less severe than if their current energy systems are starved of fuel
insights.locator: These countries may not be happy

insights.claim: The idea that Trump may inadvertently accelerate the clean energy transition is not crazy, but the transition will be an evolution rather than a revolution.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Argues against step-change transition trades sparked by geopolitical oil shocks; positions cleantech as a gradual compounding beneficiary instead.
insights.quote: But the transition will be an evolution, not a revolution.
insights.locator: The idea that Trump may inadvertently accelerate

insights.claim: China, the global champion of clean energy technology, chose to cut fossil fuel imports and thereby damp oil prices rather than maximize pain for fossil fuel consumers worldwide, which would have boosted sales of the 'new three' export industries President Xi Jinping has lauded.
insights.speaker: David M. Hart
insights.so_what: Kills the thesis that China would exploit an energy crisis to accelerate cleantech penetration — important for anyone trading cleantech on geopolitical escalation.
insights.quote: Why wouldn’t it maximize the pain felt by fossil fuel consumers worldwide, thereby boosting the sales of solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles—the “new three” export industries that President Xi Jinping has lauded
insights.locator: But that answer begs another question
